evidence: Every infrastructure definition in the committed tree (Dockerfiles, GitHub workflows, Terraform) passes checkov's vendored policy baseline at the scanned commit
expected_output: checkov-results.json (normalized: frameworks scanned, passed/failed counts, failed checks sorted) plus one observation row per failed check: check_id, check_name, framework, file, resource

assertions.description: Zero failed checks — the committed IaC matches the policy baseline, not approximately.

notes: Config-plane collector, no graph involvement by design — a Dockerfile has no call path. Frameworks are limited to what the committed tree contains (detected up front from git); a repo with nothing IaC-shaped skips honestly and the recipe stays unevidenced, never vacuously evidenced. --skip-download: the policy set inside the pinned image is the whole baseline, offline and deterministic.
caveats: Open-source checkov emits no severity — the assertion is baseline-clean, not severity-thresholded. Kubernetes manifests deferred until a consuming repo demands them.

plain.checks: Runs a fixed policy baseline over the infrastructure definitions committed to the repository — Dockerfiles, CI workflows, Terraform — and counts the checks that fail.
plain.violation: Some piece of your infrastructure is defined in a way the baseline rejects: a container with a writable root filesystem, storage without encryption, a workflow holding more permission than it uses. It is a real setting in a real file, not a note about style.
plain.fix: Every failed check names its file, its line and the policy it broke, so each one is a specific edit. A check that genuinely does not apply to you belongs in a recorded decision rather than in a silenced tool.
